title: Dow Gains 718 Points, but Divisions Run Deep
text:

https://www.barrons.com/articles/dow-gains-718-points-but-divisions-run-deep-1541810900 Dow Gains 718 Points, but Divisions Run Deep By Nov. 9, 2018 7:48 p.m. ET Order Reprints Photography by Patrick T. Fallon/Bloomberg Text size
There are two sides to every story—and that should be making investors uncomfortable right about now.
Yes, the market had a very good week. The Dow Jones Industrial Average gained 718.47 points, or 2.8%, to 25,989.30, while the S&P 500 rose 2.1% to 2781.01. The Nasdaq Composite advanced 0.7% to 7406.90. It was the Nasdaq’s first two-week winning streak since August. TK
The midterm elections presented dueling narratives of what the U.S. could and should be, and the relief when they were over was credited for the Dow’s 545-point rise on Wednesday. That gain, however, should not be seen as an endorsement of one side or the other. “The market is not a Democrat or Republican,” says David Donabedian, chief investment officer at CIBC Private Wealth Group. “You have to leave political biases aside.”
What should we be taking our cues from, if not politics? How about the Federal Reserve? It shocked no one with its statement on Thursday, which left it on track to raise rates again in December.
“While the FOMC basically said little new, it was that silence that also sent a message,” explains Peter Boockvar, chief investment officer at Bleakley Advisory Group. “It was that nothing that happened in the month of October, both market-wise and in the data, has altered their stance, and thus was an implicit confirmation of what the market has priced in for December—another rate hike.”
Trade is the other issue keeping the market stuck in place—and it’s the trickier of the two. Bank of America Merrill Lynch strategist James Barty argues that if a deal between the U.S. and China can be reached at the G20 meeting this month—even just an agreement not to increase tariffs from current levels—economists would be able to lift their 2019 global growth estimates and stocks could resume their rally. If they don’t, the stock market’s recent tumble would be validated—and then some.
“We continue to believe that the outcome of US/China trade talks is crucial to global markets,” Barty contends. “Failure would accentuate the deterioration in global growth and fully justify investors’ fears.”
And for good reason. Third-quarter earnings saw an uptick in the number of companies blaming tariffs for lackluster guidance, and we can expect more to do so the longer the trade war trundles on. But sentiment toward trade isn’t evenly split. Evercore ISI strategist Dennis DeBusschere, for one, notes that cyclical companies appear more concerned than defensive and rate-sensitive ones. And the most concerned appear to be tech and consumer-discretionary companies, DeBusschere explains—and they might get the most benefit if trade tensions ease.
They could use it. The Nasdaq, with titanic positions in companies like Apple (ticker: AAPL) and Amazon.com (AMZN), continues to lag the rest of the market, and not just last week. It’s advanced just 1.4% in November, while the Dow has gained 3.5%. Communications services, the new home of Facebook (FB), has declined 0.9% in November, while tech has risen just 0.7%. Both have lagged the energy sector, which has gained 1.7% despite the price of oil entering a bear market last week. More In Trader Steve Wynn Saved $900 Million With Well-Timed Sale of Casino Stake
Against that backdrop, how you feel about the market likely depends on how much of the potential downside you feel is already reflected in share prices. The bulls see strong U.S. economic growth, continued earnings expansion, and reasonable valuations—the S&P 500 trades at 15.9 times 12-month forward earnings, down from 18.2 times at the start of the year—as reasons for continued optimism.
Bears, for their part, point to the fact that economic growth will almost certainly decline as the boost from fiscal stimulus runs off and cite the pressure on corporate earnings from rising wages, a stronger dollar, and other factors for their pessimism. “The two camps have gotten more polarized,” says Peter Andersen of Andersen Capital Management. “It’s almost like the mirror of the political situation.”
This being the Trader column, we looked to the market for an answer—and its message is just as mixed. The S&P 500’s rally stalled at 2815.15 on Wednesday, just a hair below 2816.94, the peak after October’s waterfall decline. In technical terms, that’s called a double top. But the S&P 500 found support at its 200-day moving average near 2763 last Friday, a sign that investors aren’t ready to throw in the towel just yet. Newsletter Sign-up
All this action is happening near 2800, a level that has been the site of major market battles this year. Instinet’s Frank Cappelleri notes that the level has served as support on four occasions this year, and as resistance on five, including the most recent rally. The market might be trying to set up for a bullish reverse-head-and-shoulders pattern, but then again, it might not. “There are many factors working against a breakout,” Cappelleri explains.
We’ll stay on the cautious side until we have a better story to tell.
